concepts.name: The Greenhouse Effect: Natural vs. Enhanced Mechanism
key_dimensions: Distinction between natural greenhouse effect (life-sustaining) and anthropogenic enhanced effect (climate-disrupting)
Role of shortwave vs. longwave radiation and selective atmospheric absorption
Why Earth's average temperature would be -18°C without the natural greenhouse effect
UPSC trap: Greenhouse effect itself is not harmful — only its enhancement is

concepts.name: Carbon Dioxide (CO₂): Sources, Sinks, and Atmospheric Behaviour
key_dimensions: Natural sources (volcanic outgassing, respiration, ocean degassing) vs. anthropogenic sources (fossil fuels, deforestation, cement production)
CO₂ as the reference gas for Global Warming Potential (GWP = 1)
Carbon sinks: oceans, forests, soil — and their saturation risk
Pre-industrial concentration (~280 ppm) vs. current levels (>420 ppm) and the 'Keeling Curve' significance

concepts.name: Methane (CH₄): Sources, GWP, and Policy Significance
key_dimensions: GWP of CH₄: 28–34 over 100 years but ~86 over 20 years — UPSC trap on time-horizon dependency
Sources: enteric fermentation (livestock), paddy/rice cultivation, landfills, natural gas leaks, wetlands
India-specific relevance: rice cultivation and cattle as major CH₄ emitters
Global Methane Pledge (2021) — India's stance of not signing it and reasons why

concepts.name: Nitrous Oxide (N₂O): Agricultural Nexus and Ozone Interaction
key_dimensions: GWP of N₂O (~265–298 over 100 years) — third largest contributor by radiative forcing
Primary sources: synthetic nitrogen fertilizers, livestock manure, industrial processes (adipic/nitric acid production)
Dual role: greenhouse gas AND the dominant ozone-depleting substance in the 21st century
UPSC trap: N₂O is NOT controlled under the Montreal Protocol despite its ozone-depleting role

concepts.name: Fluorinated Gases (F-gases): HFCs, PFCs, SF₆, and NF₃
key_dimensions: Extremely high GWPs: SF₆ has GWP of ~23,500; NF₃ ~17,200 — highest among all GHGs
Sources: refrigeration/AC (HFCs), semiconductor manufacturing (PFCs, NF₃), electrical switchgear (SF₆)
Kigali Amendment to Montreal Protocol (2016): phasing down HFCs — India's ratification status and timeline
UPSC trap: F-gases have no natural sources — entirely anthropogenic, yet excluded from Kyoto Protocol's original basket for NF₃

concepts.name: Water Vapour: The Most Abundant GHG and Feedback Amplifier
key_dimensions: Water vapour contributes ~50% of the natural greenhouse effect — yet not listed as a 'controlled' GHG
Acts as a feedback (not a forcing): warming increases evaporation → more water vapour → more warming
Distinction from other GHGs: humans do not directly emit water vapour at scale that alters its global concentration
UPSC trap: Water vapour is the largest contributor to greenhouse effect but is NOT included in UNFCCC/Kyoto GHG baskets

concepts.name: Global Warming Potential (GWP): Concept, Limitations, and Application
key_dimensions: Definition: heat trapped by a gas relative to CO₂ over a specified time horizon (20, 100, or 500 years)
Why time horizon matters: CH₄ appears more dangerous over 20 years than 100 years
CO₂-equivalent (CO₂e) as a common unit for comparing and reporting national emissions
Limitations: GWP does not capture atmospheric lifetime differences or non-linear effects — alternative metric GTP (Global Temperature change Potential)

concepts.name: Ozone (O₃): Dual Role as Greenhouse Gas and UV Shield
key_dimensions: Tropospheric ozone: a GHG and air pollutant formed from NOx + VOCs + sunlight (not directly emitted)
Stratospheric ozone: protective layer — its depletion is a separate problem from climate change
UPSC trap: Ozone depletion and global warming are related but DISTINCT problems with different causative agents
Tropospheric ozone as the third-largest contributor to radiative forcing among anthropogenic GHGs

concepts.name: Black Carbon (Soot): Short-Lived Climate Pollutant and Co-Benefits
key_dimensions: Not a GHG in the traditional sense — absorbs solar radiation directly; classified as a 'short-lived climate forcer (SLCF)'
Sources: incomplete combustion — diesel engines, cooking stoves (chulhas), crop residue burning
Disproportionate impact on Himalayan glaciers and Arctic ice (albedo reduction)
Policy relevance: reducing BC offers rapid climate AND health co-benefits — India's BS-VI transition, PM Ujjwala Yojana

concepts.name: Carbon Monoxide (CO): Indirect Greenhouse Gas
key_dimensions: CO is NOT a direct GHG but an indirect one: reacts with OH radicals, reducing CH₄ oxidation → extends CH₄ lifetime
Sources: incomplete combustion, biomass burning, vehicle exhaust
UPSC trap: CO is an air pollutant AND indirect GHG — often confused with CO₂ in questions
Short atmospheric lifetime (~2 months) makes it a target for near-term climate mitigation

concepts.name: Radiative Forcing: Concept and Comparative Rankings of GHGs
key_dimensions: Definition: net change in energy flux in the atmosphere caused by a natural or anthropogenic factor (W/m²)
Ranking by radiative forcing contribution: CO₂ > CH₄ > N₂O > F-gases > Tropospheric O₃
Distinction between radiative forcing and GWP — forcing measures current impact, GWP measures cumulative potential
UPSC trap: Aerosols (sulphate) cause NEGATIVE radiative forcing (cooling effect) — masking some warming

concepts.name: Atmospheric Lifetime of GHGs: Policy and Climate Implications
key_dimensions: CO₂: effectively permanent (centuries to millennia); CH₄: ~12 years; N₂O: ~114 years; HFCs: 1–270 years
Long lifetime of CO₂ means historical emissions from developed nations still drive current warming — equity argument in UNFCCC
Short-lived pollutants (CH₄, BC) offer near-term mitigation opportunities
UPSC trap: Reducing CO₂ today will NOT immediately reduce atmospheric concentration due to carbon cycle inertia

concepts.name: Kyoto Protocol GHG Basket: Six/Seven Gases and Annexure Structure
key_dimensions: Original six gases under Kyoto (1997): CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFCs, PFCs, SF₆
Doha Amendment (2012) added NF₃ as the seventh gas for the second commitment period
Annex I vs. Non-Annex I distinction: binding targets only for developed nations — 'Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR)'
UPSC trap: India is Non-Annex I — had NO binding emission targets under Kyoto Protocol

concepts.name: India's GHG Emission Profile: Sectoral Breakdown and Global Ranking
key_dimensions: India is the 3rd largest absolute emitter but ranks ~7th in per capita emissions — crucial distinction
Sectoral share: Energy (electricity + heat) is the largest source, followed by agriculture, industry, transport
Agriculture's unique role: India's agriculture sector emits CH₄ (rice, livestock) and N₂O (fertilizers) — higher share than global average
India's cumulative historical emissions are low — central to its equity argument in climate negotiations

concepts.name: Natural Sources of GHGs vs. Anthropogenic Sources: Flux and Balance
key_dimensions: Natural carbon cycle was roughly in balance before industrialization — anthropogenic emissions disrupted the equilibrium
Wetlands are the largest natural source of CH₄; oceans are both a source and sink of CO₂
Permafrost thaw as a natural feedback source of CH₄ and CO₂ — tipping point risk
UPSC trap: Volcanoes emit only ~1% of the CO₂ that humans emit annually — often cited by climate skeptics

concepts.name: Deforestation and Land-Use Change as a GHG Source
key_dimensions: Land-use change accounts for ~10–12% of global CO₂ emissions — second largest source after fossil fuels historically
Mechanism: burning/decomposition of biomass releases stored carbon; loss of sink capacity compounds the effect
REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation): UNFCCC mechanism, India's participation
UPSC trap: Afforestation creates a carbon sink but also alters albedo — net climate benefit depends on location (tropical > temperate > boreal)

concepts.name: Rice (Paddy) Cultivation as a Source of Methane: India-Specific Issue
key_dimensions: Anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in flooded paddy fields produces CH₄ via methanogenic archaea
India is the world's second-largest rice producer — making this a nationally significant emission source
Mitigation options: alternate wetting and drying (AWD), aerobic rice, changing rice varieties
Policy tension: food security vs. climate mitigation — India's reluctance in Global Methane Pledge linked partly to this

concepts.name: Cement and Industrial Processes as Sources of CO₂
key_dimensions: Cement production releases CO₂ both from energy use (fuel combustion) and process emissions (calcination of limestone: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂)
Process emissions are harder to abate — cannot be solved by switching to renewable energy alone
Global cement industry accounts for ~8% of global CO₂ emissions
Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) and use of supplementary cementitious materials (fly ash, slag) as mitigation strategies — relevance to India's infrastructure push

concepts.name: Ozone-Depleting Substances (ODS) and Their Climate Co-Effects
key_dimensions: CFCs and HCFCs are both ODS (controlled under Montreal Protocol) AND potent GHGs — dual regulatory regime
Phase-out of CFCs inadvertently provided significant climate benefits (CFCs have very high GWPs)
HFCs were introduced as ODS replacements but are powerful GHGs — addressed by Kigali Amendment
UPSC trap: Montreal Protocol is an ozone treaty, NOT a climate treaty — yet considered the most successful climate action

concepts.name: Carbon Budget Concept and Its Equity Dimensions
key_dimensions: Carbon budget: total cumulative CO₂ emissions permissible to stay within 1.5°C or 2°C warming limits (IPCC AR6)
Remaining budget for 1.5°C is approximately 500 GtCO₂ (as of early 2020s) — shrinking rapidly
Equity dimension: developed nations have already consumed disproportionate share of the historical budget — basis for 'climate debt'
UPSC trap: Carbon budget applies to CO₂ (and CO₂e for all GHGs) — not to individual gases in isolation; often confused with carbon credits/trading
